---
title: "Appendix 3F: Interpretation in y* Metric"
---

- The binary logit model can be interpreted in three ways:
  - *y\** metric
  - Odds ratios
    - Log odds
  - Predicted probabilities
- The binary logit or probit model can be interpreted in terms of *y\**
  - This is uncommon in typical applications of the models
    - It is not the method I recommend/prefer
  - But useful to understand and used sometimes (e.g., in structural equation modeling \[SEM\])
  - Also, useful for ordinal logit/probit models (more later)
- The coefficients can be directly interpreted in terms of *y\**. Remember the model is linear in the *y\** metric

  **For a unit change in *x~k~*, *y\** is expected to change by *β~k~* units, holding all other variables constant**

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
library(haven)           # import Stata data and labels
library(dplyr)           # data manipulation

anes <- read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_anes.dta")

# Drop any missing data on the model IVs
anes <- anes[complete.cases(anes[c("age", "hhincome", "woman", "lgb", "race4",
  "edyrs", "relimport", "wrongtrack")]), ]

# Treat binary/nominal variables as factors using their value labels
anes <- anes |>
  mutate(woman = as_factor(woman), lgb = as_factor(lgb), race4 = as_factor(race4),
    relimport = as_factor(relimport), wrongtrack = as_factor(wrongtrack)) |>
  droplevels()

logitmod <- glm(vote_trump ~ hhincome + edyrs + woman + lgb + race4 + relimport +
  wrongtrack + age + I(age^2), family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = anes)
summary(logitmod)
```

:::

> *Each additional year of education leads to a 0.140 decrease in y\* (propensity to vote for Trump)*
>
> *Women are about 0.35 lower on y\* (propensity to vote for Trump) than men*

## Example y\* interpretations

*"The problem with this interpretation is that the variance of y\* is unknown, so the meaning of a change of **β~k~** in y\* is unclear." ([Long 1997](https://us.sagepub.com/en-us/nam/regression-models-for-categorical-and-limited-dependent-variables/book6071) p.70)*

- Results from a binary probit model illustrate Long's point:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
probitmod <- glm(vote_trump ~ hhincome + edyrs + woman + lgb + race4 + relimport +
  wrongtrack + age + I(age^2), family = binomial(link = "probit"), data = anes)
summary(probitmod)
```

:::

## y\* standardized interpretations

- One solution is to *y\** standardize the coefficient; i.e. put it in standard deviation of *y\** units
- First, need to calculate the variance/standard deviation of *y\**

$$\widehat{Var}(y^{*}) = \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}' Var(\mathbf{x}) \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} + Var(\varepsilon)$$

- Where the variance of the error is assumed (1 in probit; π^2^/3 in logit)
- Then, put coefficient in *y\** standard deviation units:

$$\beta_{k}^{Sy*} = \frac{\beta_{k}}{\sigma_{y*}}$$

**For a unit increase in *x~k~*, *y\** is expected to increase by $\boldsymbol{\beta_{k}^{Sy*}}$ standard deviations, holding all other variables constant**

### y\* standardized coefficients

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
# Latent SD: variance of the linear predictor + variance of the error
sd_ystar_logit <- sqrt(var(predict(logitmod, type = "link")) + pi^2 / 3)
sd_ystar_probit <- sqrt(var(predict(probitmod, type = "link")) + 1)
c(logit = sd_ystar_logit, probit = sd_ystar_probit)

# y* standardized coefficients
data.frame(b_logit = coef(logitmod), bStdY_logit = coef(logitmod) / sd_ystar_logit,
  b_probit = coef(probitmod), bStdY_probit = coef(probitmod) / sd_ystar_probit)[-1, ] |>
  round(4)
```

:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"}
*y\** coefficients differ noticeably; *y\** standardized coefficients **are virtually identical in both logit and probit model**

- Each additional year of education is associated with a 0.05 standard deviation decrease in the propensity to vote for Trump
- Compared to men, women are 0.127 standard deviations lower on propensity to vote for Trump
:::

## Advice on y\* interpretations

- *y\** interpretations only really make sense if you think an underlying latent continuum exists and you can name and talk about it cogently
- Standardized coefficients are useful to facilitate comparisons across models: all are on the same standard deviation scale
  - If you are going to use *y\** interpretations, I recommend *y\** standardized coefficients
- Ultimately, the interpretations are not very satisfying as the substantive magnitude of an effect is unclear---even with *y\** standardized coefficients
  - I find marginal effects a better default interpretation strategy (see [3.6 Marginal Effects](3-6-marginal-effects.qmd))
